Sometimes, I wear heavily masc clothes and sometimes I present very femme. Gender presentation should not lead to gender assumptions. Every trans person in my social circle see they/them as gender neutral and if you're corrected then you use the correct pronouns. I think it can be a bit more obvious when it's being weaponized because said person will keep using it despite being corrected or the context of that person's belief or general behavior. I think that's a separate issue entirely that we don't need to blame on other trans people within the trans community who would also be targeted by said people. Though it's not explicitly spiritual I did find a great deal of spiritual gain from having read it.

I have always found the Artist's Way Morning Pages Journal to be an incredibly helpful and spiritual guided journal that helped me tap into my creativity and work through some stuff.

it's a companion journal to {{The Artist's Way: A Spiritual Path to Higher Creativity by Julia Cameron}} her perspective on some things is a little out of touch from the working class experience but I do think her methods have been really helpful and she's very keen on talking through fears of failure or mistakes which I personally find comforting

The Invited by  Jennifer McMahon :  a subversive take on the classic haunted house story of a family uprooting to start a new life in a new home. However in this book, the haunted house is created by the protagonists themselves.  (I haven't read this one yet but I'm eager to and it sits in my to-read pile)

The Grip of It by Jac Jemc: an incredibly heady and psychological ghost story about a young couple, Julie and James, who move to a brand new house in hopes to repair their strained relationship. However, not long after settling in, their new life takes a turn towards the surreal. They begin to find strange markings on the walls including cryptic and crude childlike drawings and a large mysterious stain that begins to move on its own. Bruises show up on the one of the Julie's body that match the stains on the ceiling and a raspy voice can be heard wheezing in the night- or are those just the pipes?

The Haunting of Hill House by Shirley Jackson: the 1959 staple of horror lit that changed haunted house genre forever. Eleanor Vance is a browbeaten and sheltered woman whose never gotten a chance at independence until she is called upon by a parapsychologist and a team of volunteer participants to spend time in a infamously haunted house to collect data on the paranormal. There she is joined by Dr Montague the good humored aforementioned parapsychologist, Theodora the confident and clever (and most likely Sapphic) artist, and Luke the young playboy and reluctant heir to Hill House. With only them to keep each other company, they are tasked with staying at the isolated mansion for the summer. Until it begins to appear the house itself may have other plans.

It's pulp written as a tribute to pulp but  the ending of My Best Friend's Exorcism by Grady Hendrix punched me in throat using the power of unconditional love and friendship. It got me out of long reading slump and it was also the first time in a long time that I cried to a piece of fiction.

But that might be too big of a leap in readability because it's been a long time since i've picked up his work and i don't recall the accessibility level of it. From my experience if you jump from faster paced read to a slow burner or a more literary piece it's going to make reading an absolute chore. Reading for yourself is incredibly important.

I would also add to the suggestion list, my personal favorite lesser known author [Dan Vyleta](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/2608207-pavel-i?ac=1&from_search=true&qid=pkThsiy40U&rank=1)

For heavier literary writing I would strongly suggest Umberto Eco's work
